It ie easy to true out the tra- ditional relics of this water ord.al, in the ignorant barbarity Oat practisol in many countries to discover witch., by casting them mb spool of water, and drowning them to prove their innocence. In the Eastern empire tire fire ordeal was used for the woe pupa., by tbe emperor Theodore Lascaria who, attributing bill sickness to magic, caused all those whom be sospested to handle the hot teas; thus j. mg (as hes been well rerearketlt. to the mom dubious< in the world tin most dubious proof of innocence. Boat. these methods of trials, there were some others common to. Europe; as the judicial combat, the od.l of the crow, and the ordeal of the aimed. Dr. Henry gives the fellowiug eceemat of it,—"ln crinintal trials., the judgment of the crow was maroon!, thus audoeted. When the primmer had declared his innounee upon oath, and appealed to tbe judgment of the cross, two sticks were prepared exactly like one another; the figure of the cross was cut on one of these kirks, and nothing on the Other; each of them waa thee wrapped up in a quantity of fine white wool, and laid on the altar, or on the relies of the saints; after which • solemn prayer wu put up to God, that he would be pleased to die. oover, bv evident signs, whether the prisoner was innocent or guilty. These solemnities being finiesed, • pricer ap- proached the altar, and took up one of these sticke, which wan uncovered with reach anxiety. If it waa the stick marked with the cron, the priouner wupronounced innocut, If it yr. the other, he was declared guilty." When the judgment of the cross was appealed to, in civil causes, the trial was conducted in thin manner :—.The judger, wile., and all concerned, being assembled too church, each of the parties chose a priest, the youngest and atouteet that he conlel find, to be lois representative in lit. trial. These repro. eentatives were then placed one on each side of some famous crucifix ; and, at • eignal give, they both at owe stretched their arms at full length, so aa to form • cross with their body. In this painful posture they continued to stand while divine service was performing; and the party whose representative dropped his arms first lost his cause. These, and the like relics of sumwathion and barbarism, were aboliehedin England (as had been done in Denmark aboe• • century before), by Act of Parliament 3 Henry 111. ac- cording to Sir Edward Coke, or rather by an order of the king in council. We have, in If, Turner's well.known History of the Anglo-Saxons, a full account of the ordeals in nee among that people trona the tau of Ina. "The iron," mys 31r. Turno' was to be three pounds in weight for the threefold Pia', and therefore probably one pound only for the more simple charge; and the accused was to have the option, whether he would prefer the water ordeal or the Iron ordeal. No man was to go within the church after the Ore was lighted by which the ordeal was to be heated, en- Copt the erten and the accused. The distance ~f inne fro was to be then measured out, from the stake, of the length of the foot of the accused. If the trial waa to be by hot water, the water was heated till it toiled furiously ; and the vestel that contained it was to be iron or copper, lead or clue. If the charge was of the kind they oallnt anfeald, or simple, the accused was to interne his hand as for as the wrist in the water, to take out the do. ; if the charge was of a threefold magnitude, lie was to plunge his arm up to the elbow. When the ordeal was ready, two men were to enter of each side, and to agree that the water was boiling furiouely. Then an equal number°, men were to enter from each side, and to stand along the church on both sides of the ordeal, all feet- , ing. After this the pried was to sprinkle them with holy I water, of which each was to WU; they were to ki. the , • compete, and to be 'signed with tho crow All this tinte the fire was not to be mended any more; but the iron, if the ordeal was to be by hot iron, wu to lie on the coals till the last collect was finished; and it was then to be placed on the . staples which were to sustain it. While the eccueed Woe , snatching the stone out of the water, or carrying the hot . iron for the Apace of nine feet, nothing was to be said but • . prayer to the Deity to discover the truth. The hand wee , to be then hound un rind evaled, and to lo kept so for three day,; after that time the seal and the leindekee were re- i moved, and the Land Woo to be !unlined to see whether it , was foul or clear. "I assorew," said the Queen in her speech at the prorogation of Parliament on Tuesday, "to observe that, notwithstanding the lateuem of the period at which you began your labours, your indefatigable zeal and patients, have enabled you to add to the , statute book some valuable laws." To the drawback of the latestem of the period at which legislatorn began their labours her Majesty might have added that of the unconacionable and unpardonable petty obstruction which the members of the Third and ,• Fourth parties in the lions° of Common., and which certain peers, out of a selfish perverse spirit in the House of Lords, offered to attempts of the Government to "add to the statute book some valuable laws," of which both England and Ireland stood much in need. The first emaion of the new Parliament, which was brought to a close on Tuesday, assembled on the 20th of May, after oae of the most decisive victories fur the policy saran- seated by Mr. Gladetone ever achieved in the electoral boothe either by Liberals or Conservatives. The I Howie of Commons was made up of 900 Liberals, ! 240 Conservatives, and 60 Home Rulers. The Queen's opening speech sot forth the deter- mination of the new Ministry, under the guidance cf Mr. Gladstone, to put on the statute book "the valuable lawn" which her Majeety's speech of Tuesday last declared had been put on. The epoech at the begiming of the eession announced e prormed establishment of a European concert with • view to "the early and complete fulfilment of the Treaty of Berlin with respect to effectual reforms and equal laws in Turkey, as well as to snob territorial questions as have not been settled :" the pacification of Afghanistan and south Africa, the restoration to order and solvency from a state of ohsos of the Indian finances which, under the governorship of Lord Lytton, had been extraordinarily muddled ; the non•neceseity to renew the Peace Preservation Act, which had nearly run it. limit ; the settlement of the burials controversy, the renewal of the Ballot Act; the protection of occupiers of land against injury from ground game; the determination on a just principle of the liabilities of employers for aceidenta sustained by workmen : and the exteneion of the borough franchise in Ireland. Notwithstanding—as the speech of Tues- day last declared, and might have declared—the late- noes of the period when legislation began, and the unwarrantable obstruction offered, nearly the whole of We programme has been carried out. The European concert la a reality; and though the Sick Man, of the Sublime Porte, has been slow to carry into effect the I Berlin Treaty, the Powers which signed that treaty , have brought, and will bring, pressure to bear on Turkey to obtain a satisfactory settlement of the Greek I and Montenegrin frontier question, the administra- tive organisation of the European provinces of Turkey, and the principal reforms required in the Aaiatio provineee inhabited by Armenians. Them are few who will not concur with the Powers in the belief that by their united action to compel Turkey to fulfil the terms of the Treaty they are doing that which is "best caleidated to insure tranquility in the East." The pacification of Afghanistan and South Africa haa not been accomplished it is true but the brilliant victory secured by Sir F. Roberts and his gallant troop.; over Ayoub Khan before Candahar promises to. be the beginning of the end of that miserable and unjust interference with the Afghans, whilst, as to' South Africa, we are told that the general state of affairs is now on the whole satisfactory, extept in Basutoland, where Iler Majesty truism that a moderate and conciliatory policy may allay the agitation caused by the enforcement in the carrying out of the epirited foreign policy" of the late Government— of the Disarmament Act. The Education Act has re- ceived amendment; the law of burials, which is not yet wholly satisfactory, has, m well as the Act for the better determining the liability of employers, passel through the ordeal of wilful obetraction in the House of Common, and inconsistent tinkering in the House of Lord,, and been enrolled among the nation's etatutee The Hares and Rabbits Bill, after being subjected to treatment similar to that extended to the Burial. Bill and the Liability of Employers Bill by the so• called "farmers' friends," has passed into law and in six months the present Government has eon- ferred upon the tenant farmers a boon winch the " farmers' friends " never attempted, dewing the whole of the Biz years they were in Ale, to concede. The abolition of the Malt Tex —mother boon to the fanning interest—was accomplished by • Gleahitonian budget, which wrought consternation in the ranks of the Con- servatives and evoked the warmeet admiration from the Liberal supporters of the Government. The paesage of the Savings Bank Act, the Poet Office Orders Act, the measures to regulate the wages of seamen and to promote the safer carriage of grain cargoes, may be among the smaller accomplishments in the Govern- ment's achievements, but they are such as were needful, and will not only meet with public approval, but will be found practical nee/ ul statutes. TERRIBLE COLLIERY DISASTER.
BIIINGING UP THE DEAD.

• (Conti.ed fro.. petit 3.) Writing from Seaharn Harbour at ten o'clock yeaterday morning, a correspondent says, this has been a long an'el dreary night for the officials at the month of the pit. and the few reporters who are anxiously watching for any signs of the recovery of bodice The private intimation wan that,before ten o'clock lust night there were eleven corpses at the bottom tithe shaft, and that when the large concourse of persons who had collected dispereed thy would be raised, I True to their arrangement, Mn. ntratton. finding the engine- I house fire so well under, made an attempt to lift the tuba, but a hitch at once occurred in the gear, end it was not until live minetse past 'to this morning, that the first victim. of the diuster were brought to the bank. The bodies had been identified in the pit, and were then seen up in canvas. They were afterwards ,limbled up inn info, and, in the usual style of colliers coming to the surface, the arms were placed over the side, the means of eecurity adopted being tying the bead, to the chain hoisting the tub. In this manner were the drat two bodies of the victiins of the Seaham exploaion brought to the surface, and. twenty live minutes later up came the tub again w ith two more corpses, Med things proceeded as they had begun, bribe time of writing many more would hese hcen recovered, bet at 2-40 there I I came an alarm of fire, ands request to send down the hose, I I the condagration in the engine-house having again broken lout. So extensive were the dames this time the, was not until nearly ten o'clock that the rnen who came up were able to report tE.,t the pit nie again cold, and that the work of , bringing up the dead could I.e gone on with. Meanwhile , the reuuins of the four I have mentioned have been ron ! moved to their hornes in coffins already on ate in the joiner'. I shop. A few of the men who formed the last exploring party state that they have been Doane way bat No. 1 steam, land bad found four men, and one was so badly mutilated , that be could not be identified. They recognised others. however. These were at once taken iotbohofjotnntttoe , shaft for removal to the bank when put in canvas. Other I , bodies. were al AO come across, but they could not Le got out , or recognised. Every arrangement has been made for I , bringing those found to the surface, but the main pit work I will be done it the quietest possible manner. especially as the remains of those found recentlyare dreadfully mutilated, limbs having teen strewn in all directions, while the heads lot two or three have been blown off. Unless the cages can I be set to work Nirly the whole of those sent up will lure to I come in the tuba. It waa to avoid this that the officials have deLeyed a little, and have repaired the shafts, but the relatives were becoming loud in their demands for the too..

Writing an hour lat, (II o'clock) a correspondent says Since my last desmatch seven bodies have been brought to the surface, but they are so diefigured that only two have . been identified, and thews are two of the men mentioned as , having been seen by one of the explorers. I have just been in the house set apart for the dead, end can quite understand the exclamation of horror of even old colliers. Each corpse ,is burnt to a cinder. Two have lost bead.; arms and legs are miming, and up to the present anxious relative. wlm have been in say they cannot recognise any as their friends. Meanwhile, to add to tile difficulties with which the rescuing parties are surrounded, Mr. Corlett, the chief agent to Lord Londonderry, has just receive' news of another dreg No. 3 ventilating (enlace. dre at the veutileting furnace is giving more tnoble than was enticipand, and it is feared that some time must elapse before it is put out. Meanwhile much larger numbere of men are going down, the object being to clear the workings as soon as possible, and repair the damages. I have jest bad uconneneattin with Mr. Boyd, the check viewer of mine, which pay royalties to the dean one chapter of Durham he is doing duty at the pit's mouth in turn with other gentlemen from the locality. Mr. Ifalyd informs me that he hue sent two mtweages below to the effect that all bodies, found are ta be at once sent up. and he has ar- ranged to hare colTuis at the surface in which to place those which may be identified. The twelfth body has jure been I brought to the surface. Inquiries as to the discrepancy in I the number said to be in the pit and the number of lamp. Mailed have let to the information that two Movemen and ' two packers. who work in wire, have three hinge given I them, in case an extra one should be required. and the depu- ties also are provided with a second light. This might ac- count for a few, but the authoritim Ray they are certain that 147 bodies are in the pit at the present time Ae I write a broken Davy lamp Las been brought up from the mein coal seam, and. baa been placed under lock and key. The relatives of the miner, in the pit continue to arrive at the c,fficoa opened by the Northumberland and Durham Miners' Ferinauent Relief Fund to lodge particulars of their claim.

-lEAMAN, 1.30 r ~—The melancholy work of bringing bodies to the surface is now progreseing as fast nn can he ex- pected, the total above ground having been reieed Co ' teen. The people seem to be very much relieved at the pro- gresa made in the recovery of the dead, and the pit wears. very different aspect to what it did on Thursday. The fire at No. 3 ventilating furnace has now been got under.

Dr. McDorps. moved an amendment that the further con- sideration of the matter he deferred for twelve months. There would beno advantage either to the Board or the rate. papei sby the appoiMment of such a committee. It would be nothing but an impotent mockery to appoint a Parlia- mentary Committee when there was no Parliamentary work for it to do. No reasons had been given why such • committee should be appoin. ed, and in his opinion it was calculated to to infinite mischief, because they would be appointed with a wide range, and might do what another committee had done before them, via., ride roughshod over the rights Alla privileges of the ratepayer.. He could not conceive why the Hoard should allow itself to be led into appointing a committee like that. And what w s the Parliamentary Committee to do? SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN LADY. At the Runcorn Town Hall, en Monday, before Mr. W. Henke. (chairman') and Mr. 8 B. Chadwick. Mrs. Mary . Haddock, a lady owning • eensidarablei mount of house property in the town, aged 64, ems charged with haring, on tbePwwinns SetftnlPY, einkes four ;mends of beef, value So. &1., the property of Yr. Owen Lloyd, butcher.of Chester,' who visits Runcorn on Saturdays. The court was crowded. Amonpt those present were the Rey. W. Robinson, curate of Trinity Church, and the Rey. Henry Valentine, Wesleyan Methodist. Mr. Day, and Mr. Labe were 'yoth present, &gel the latter gentleman repreeented the Klepper, who had been allowed out on bail. She appeareel very collected. Mr. Lloyd said he was* butcher, and bad • shop at 22, elllighwt. He had two partner., one Robert Willis, and the other John Lloyd.. brother. They had only one shop in Runcorn, which wan open on Saturday. only. It was open on the previous Saturday, in the afternoon of which day he cow the prisoner standing at the shop window, which was open. There was • table in the window bettom, on which they placed their meat. There were three people standing there while he was weighing a piece of meat on the scales Inside the shop. Ile was standing sideways to the window. and wee in such • position that he could not nee the pri. sonar's Um, neither could she see his. There were come hind quarters of mutton hanging from the tear in the window. In a short thne he cow the prisoner put out flee hand land take up the piece of sirloin of beef produced from the win. dose bottom, and place it under vet shawl. As noon as he saw the meat ge he no woe I down and saw that it was the the prisoner who had taken it. Ile then went to his brother, who was also in the shop, and told Ihno in a whteperto fetch policenssn. His brother at once went out, and as soon as he had done no the prisoner came into the shop with other people. There WAS some meat on the block m the shop, and when she Calail) in sloe commenced to look at it. One was a piece of chine, which would we'd,' siont font or hen pounds. While she was Waling at the meat the policeman came in near to where the prisoner win standing. He (witness) said to him, "Officer, this lady has got a piece of meat that she has mken mg of the window "The 0.411er turned round to the officer, and said "Oh dear don', take me. toil! give You anything to let one off." IP (witness) said, 00 gi,„ in change to you." The officer told her she must go with him. Wnen he told the edicer she had got • piece of beef he caught hold of her and pulled her shawl ankle, and the piece of beef was naen partly in the hog and partly out. Ile bad seen the pri.oner at the slim on other Saturdays, but did not know that she had ever tourch wed anything. They hail been cautioned to keep their even,,. a person in black, which canoed him to notice more particularly what took place. The piece of heel wan worth 30. They never gave credit to their customers in Runcorn. Sergeant Cashin mid that shoe three o'clock on Satur- day afternoon last, the prosecutor's brother earns to him while standing near his Mop, and asked him to go rside. lie did so, and now the lent witness l'rosecutor looked straight at the witness, who wan near to the block with a number of other people, and said, " That lady has rot a lump of beef which she has taken out of the window." She turned round to hirn immadiately with her right hand under her shawl. He (witness) pulled it anide and saw she had the bag produced under her left arm, and had hold of the piece of beef which was Mehl.. He caught hold of the bag, and the presecittor said he would give her in charge Th. prisoner " For liotTe Flake, don't take me! twill pay Ton anything Onion me go, I will p,y anything you want for the beef." That was said while she looked towards Lloyd. He was endeavouring to get her from the shop. She was crying, and in a few &mats she said," I only took it from the board to take it in the chop to get it weighed." He (witness) mid it I,la very funny Co put it into the big to get it weighed ; but you must come to the Town Ilell to settle it there." She replied, " If it wan in the bag you put loin." He then took her to the police stdion, where, in anmeer to the charge, she said she did not Intend to steal the beef, and would pay for it. Mr. Lake, for the defence, mid that co doubt the prose. elation bad put their c.,se into the best possible Corm they could ; but he thought the Benet] would agree with him that the charge was a most trumpery one. The evidence was that the prosecutor stw the woman take a piece of heel from the bench, which w.ts really the most convenient place Or get it too person outside of Ow shmo. It war a very com- mon thing for people who were buying meat to pick apiece op for the purpose of seeing whether it would to for them or not. Mrs. Haddock WM posing the chop and am a piece of beef which appeared to the very one site wanted. The witneseen bad ahnitted that the chop was very crowded, anal there was Also a large 'mother of perwins outside of it. Very likely this was a very gaol piece of beef that some of the other people might have taken a liking to, and in order to secure it, she picked it up and took it into the shop. Ile uked the magi:grates wiuther it was at all reasonable that • person who wished to steal apiece of beef, would lake it off the window sill. and then walk right into the seller'. den with it. In order to constitute the offence there were thrm thing, necessary. First, it !stunt he proved that the prisoner had taken the meat into her possession ; secondly, that she had carried it away and thirdly, that there wane felonious intent. He wan prepared, on the part of his client, to admit that she did take up the idece of heel, and carried it into the shop; but he denied that there notary felonious intent wherever to take it.apart from paying for The lady instructed him that she asked "What will be the price of this piece of beef.n lt must be remembered that the shop was wry crowded at the time, and that the lady might have asked and not received an answer to her ques- tion. The prosecutor slated thd, without asking his client a single question aleaut the piece of beef, he sent his brother for a policeman, and on his arrival immailiately gave her in charge. The lady never denied honing the beef. She was 64 years of age, and a woinan of her years would naturally be more nervous than 0 younger person would bet and when charged with an offence of this character she said, For Gml's Atka don't take me. I will ply anything or do anythint, ir you will only tot me off." 01 course they all knew how very dinagmeable ands...lolls a matter it was for. lady of her respectability to even have such a charge pre- ferred agiinst her. Site wits a woman of imlependent means, and at the very time when the chttge was preferred she had nom. her the sum of 24s Ad He submitted to their woes AM. I hat it was most unlikely that a person like her would Meal a piece of beef, of the val. of Its. 111., as there wan not the slight.kt necessity for her obtaining goods in the manner suggest...l by the prosacntion. The police-sergeant in his evidence admitted that his client told him she nark the beef into the ehop for theopurp 'roof having it weighed. The fact of it being found in the hog might appear rather suspicious. H, would explain this by saying that the woman sem carrying the bag toy the handle, and she would naturally mop.oee that her hot hand would not improve the state of the meet She consequently rested the beef against the hog, and, an she was going ir o the sloop, the other women jostled her m that it slipped further into the bag. If she had had any ,eel intention to steal the beef she would have pot it altogether nut of sight, and the shawl she had In her hand wonld cosily have covered it. He maintained thot the ease was one highly ionpr,olatble upon Hoe very face of it ; hut he would not leave it there. brit call witnesses who would tell them that the woman wan of the highest respec- tability and honesty, and utterly ineapable of the offence with which she was charged. After doing so, he felt sore their worships would see thair way to dismissing the ease, and to declaring before a crovnled court that his client left the building without the slightent imputation upon her diameter. Or. McDougall said he load known the prisoner for 12 yes,, and she had always borne an excellent character. Peroonally, he believed it was perfectly impossible ten her to he guilty of snob an act as that with which ahe was &sewed;

The MM.:AL OrVICFII said he had to report an it.crease in the mortality of the borough, caused by the great heat and dryness, of the season. No rain fell for 28 days, and the brook was nmrly dried up. In con.- quence of this state of things the sewerage of the town bad not famed away from the borough. Diarrlams had prevailed, no fewer than 37 cases of death having taken place in the month. Fever woe very rife, chiefly of a typhoid character. The inspector, the mediml officer said, vint all cases known to .131. So far the dmths had been few. It the town sewers were flooded by some stored op water in all dry weather those cases at diarrhrea and fever would be fewer in number and leas in character.

The statement of deaths for the month ending September 4th showod that there had been eight deathe from whooping cough, three fever, 37 diarrlwea, two other aymoties. There had been 124 deaths from all muses. Of them 84 were males; 60 were female.; BS being children under five ymrs of age. The rate of mortality W. 19 2802, as compared with 17 63 in the mrreepontling month of last year. During the month there had been 1119 birthe.

Lyons bottle works has been caused by the acid in the brook danuaing the roof al the arch. As you are perfectly aware the Corporation have ncr right to allow acid to be turned into the brook, we must hold them responsible for the damage done. The matter being urgent we have put the work in our solicitor's hand, and will fur- nish you with a stotetnent of the c od of restoring the arch when coinpleted." , . .

Mr. HART said if the arch gave way to the aunt extent as a portion of it had been doing, the town would be loon- , dated with water. There would alo be such a frightful stench from it. One of his men went down the other day, and in consequence was a long time ill. They were putting it in repair, and would furnish the Corporation with the cost.

Mr. Haar said that the Globe Alkali Company had during the past month placed obstructions in the brook be- low their works, which had caused a considerable rise in the brook near there, sufficient to cover up the outlet of their druin, than preventing samples being taken. Ile wrote them requesting iminediate removal of the same, and this request wrc partially complied with. The following correspondence I had passed between them :—.C.entlemen,—l find to-day I your men have again placed an obstruction in the brook be- tween the bridges, thereby stopping the flow and raising the level of the water—au act calculated to cause very serious mischief, and in opposition to the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869. A few days ago we removed the obstruction first placed therein. and I now must respect( tiny request you to at once remove the obotructions put in and allow the dew of the brook to go on without interruption. The Corpo- ration are most anxious to keep the condition of the brook as perfect and sanitary as possible, hence the desirability of a speedy compliance with the above requirement.—l am, gentlemen, vow- obedient servant, J.ktillte ttose"

. ..... A furtl;ei letter was sent by the surveyor asking the immediate removal of the obstruction, or be would be obliged to clear it away, as it was of great importance that the brook should not be impeded in its flow not altered in the fall. In reply to these epistles the following letter from the Globe Alkali Company, dated September 2nd, was received Dear sir,—We have your letters of yesterday and to-der'. We are not aware of own obligation on our part to keep a clear course in the Sankey brook, although we presume a portion of it is our private property. We know nothing of the impediment you spook of, and most therefore refer you to those who have causod the obstruc- tion. As the supply of water to the works has been very much interfered with by obstruction front the canal com- pany, and other works higher up the br.fk, we are glad to hear you have the power to interfere, and shall feel much obliged try your doing it. As the brook has been a drain to been works for the last 20 years or more, you most bear in mind that we have a preacriptive right to the use of the water end al, to drain fate it. If the Corporation desire to keep the brook perfect and sanitary as you may, slope should be taken to prevent the flow of alkali waste liquor into it, which is the great cause of huisance. Yours truly,
.... —.Mr. Mane mid that on the receipt of :he last letter he tent his men and carts and cleared away the obstruction altogether.

Mr. E. llo—ugh—tO.n, assistant nuisance inspector, submitted his report on the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen, he., for the past month, and begged to state that the escape from brooks on both sides of the town had been anything but on the decline. On August 26th be noticed a very rapid change of colour in brook in Gne Works Yard, at a quarter to eleven it was a light brown, and was acid, but at eleven a.m, it was quite black and not en strongly acid. On the same date, at 11-35 now, be found sulphurettwl hydrogen in large quantity by Lyons' Bottle Works, so strong as almost to drive him away from the archway of the brook. lie found the smell of sulphuretted hydrogen very strong on !several occasions on passing along Warrington New- road, near to the open length of brook in the Gas Works Yard. On August 31/th the sal- phuretted hydrogen being liberated in Ravenhead inanhole was very bad indeed. The Rainford Brook hod been in a worse state this last seven or eight days than ever he re- membered having soen it this last twenty live years. Tam- pering with the water couree by way of putting in drain. have in no way improved things, as when these were re- moved the I iqnor, which was distinctly acid, came in a large volume in contact with waste drainage, and then the stink was very bad indeed. Residents in Park-rood complained about the etench from the brook last Wednesday night, sod it was not to be wondered at, if they had it anything like what it wa• in the centre of the town. The Town !fall and vicinity were completely enveloped in a mixture of gas.

Ann Broad,. a married woman, WAS charged with stealing coal. value Id., front the Carr', Colliery Company, on Friday, the 27th police officer stated that lie saw the woman coming from the premises of the prosecutorn, having under her shawl the coal produced. She carried it atom IS yards. but recognising him (the officer) she put it down, and said to the officer that she wanted the coal to show to her little girl what sort of coal she had thrown away.—Joerph Story, the yard foreman at the Caere Colliery Co., said the women in the neighbourhood had been in the habit of " picking coal from a ruhbiah heap and the company was determined to put A atop to it.—Mr. Spencely elicited from witness that the coal produced wan of an inferior unality and was not sold to the cushainers but it was picked mg of the rubbish heap by boys and burnt At the "Ore holes." The CLERK read the following letter—" Local Govern- ment Hoard Whitehall, 7th September, 1880.—Sir,-1 am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to their ,1 letter to you of the 30th July lard ; and to transmit to you for the information of the Guardians of the Warrington , Union, the accompanying extract from the report which the , Board have received from their inspector, Dr. Monet, of his , visit to the workhouse, and temporary school, on the sth ult. I Jun directerl to etam that when the report hoe been I considered by the Guardians it will be satiefactory to the Hoard to be Informed of the viewe of the Guardians upon I , the eubject. and of the eteps which they may propose to I . take to remedy the defects pointed ditt by Dr. Monet.—l am, err, At., Edward Sutton, assistant-secretary. ,1 In the extract Dr. Moult stated he fleet visited the wanly • of the workhouse infirmary, in which the tick children weed , treated, and Rob. quently the converted store rooms am ! ediff sergeent, quartern of the militia barracks, where th I ' rest of the children were. lie examined every sick child' I and mw all thom no, on,the sick list at a general parade. The dimmer, fern which those on the medical relief register , were labouring were ecabies porrigo or ecald head two or , three yesca of nplithalmia, and a few example, of other ekin eruptions. The first mentioned were all more or less cora- -1 trek,. and commenicable, and their continuance and spread j were due to unfavourable hygienic conditions. The general health of ail the children, however, appeared good. The arrangemen. of the workhouse inti-mary were nod well , adapted for their proper treatment. In addition to the I very grave objection of their being mixed up with the I adult, the beds and bedding, the washing and latrine ar. rangementa, the supply of brushft, combo, and towels. and the nursing were not utisfactory. Prodigel cleanlinoes, , more or leer complete separation of all cams of ophthalmia, , porde°, and scab., sad exceptional care and skill on the part of the nurses were needed to eradicate them diseases.. These conditions he did not find in the tickwards of the infl,mary. That state of things must be the normal con- dition of the workhouse as respected the sick children, and hod no nerevary cennection with their rely oval le the bar- rack, which was eituated at a dietance of about a mile from the workhouse. The wmbing arrangements were extremely , insoffieient and unsatisfactory, and the night arrangementn I for the natural wants of those children who needcd a proper place of report, were Very objectionable. The arrangements for bathing the sick children were equally defective, and the deep slate deaths very ill adapted for the purport, as the younger children cannot be placed in it conveniently for waehing. He ventured toexpress hie surpriee that the sick children should he placed in no uneeitable a portion of the workhouse as the preeent iefirmary. while there was much better accommodation available. At the Barrack, he found a single, large. omen yard. nins. yards by sixty, with a cur. face of loose mode.. In the main building which appeared to have been a store, the upper rooms were used as school roome, and on the lower door, in small compartments, the toys slept. eight in each.
